1.title: Requirements, Life Cycle and Software Engineering Foundations
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Requirements, Life Cycle and Software Engineering Foundations. This module covers the skills understanding requirements, systems life cycle, software engineering foundations. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. Turning business requirements into functional, non-functional and infrastructure requirements for a Claude application. The systems life cycle for an L L M (large language model) application, including evals, versioning and retirement. Software engineering foundations: R E S T A P I s (application programming interface) and Jason (Java Script Object Notation), asynchronous programming, version control, S D L C integration, code review, refactoring.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater Insurance Wants a Claims Assistant
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater Insurance Wants a Claims Assistant. Business goal: "Cut the time adjusters spend reading claim files". Constraints: files hold personal data, adjusters wait for answers, and the budget is limited. Your job: turn that sentence into requirements a team can build and test.

1.title: Understanding Requirements
1.text: Understanding Requirements. Requirements start from the business requirement and the solution architecture. Split them into three kinds. Functional. Question it answers: What must the system do? Claims assistant example: Summarize a claim file, answer questions about a policy, cite the source page. Non-functional. Question it answers: How well, how fast, how safely, at what cost? Claims assistant example: First answer in under five seconds, cost per claim under a limit, answers grounded in the file, P I I protected. Infrastructure. Question it answers: Where and on what does it run? Claims assistant example: Which A P I platform (first-party or a cloud provider), region and data residency, rate limits and capacity, secrets storage, logging.

1.title: Understanding Requirements, continued
1.text: Understanding Requirements, continued. The figure shows this: From business requirement to functional, non-functional and infrastructure requirements, then to acceptance criteria that become evals. Every requirement needs a measurable acceptance criterion (a number or a pass or fail check). Those criteria become your evals (Module sixteen). The classic L L M trade-off is quality, latency and cost: you rarely maximize all three, so rank them from the requirement. Waiting users drive latency; overnight work drives cost.

1.title: Understanding Requirements, continued
1.text: Understanding Requirements, continued. Requirements also decide the A P I choice (real-time or batch), the model tier and whether tools or retrieval are needed. Exam tip: In a requirement-driven question, underline the binding constraint (latency, cost, compliance, data residency) and choose the option that satisfies that constraint first. Exam tip: A requirement without a measurable acceptance criterion cannot become an eval, so it is not yet a requirement.

1.title: Systems Life Cycle
1.text: Systems Life Cycle. The figure shows this: The life cycle of a Claude application: requirements, design, build, test with evals, deploy, operate and monitor, maintain, retire, then back to requirements.

1.title: Systems Life Cycle, continued
1.text: Systems Life Cycle, continued. Requirements and design. Pick A P I, model, tools; write acceptance criteria. Build. Prompts, tools, schemas and configuration live in version control. Test. Evals with graded examples run on every change; unit tests for tool code. Deploy. Pin the model version; roll out gradually; feature-flag prompt changes. Operate. Monitor quality, latency, cost, error rates; log request I Ds and traces. Maintain. Update prompts, dependencies and models; re-run evals; handle model retirement. Retire. Migrate before the model's retirement date; archive data. Prompts are code: version them, review them, test them, and roll them back.

1.title: Systems Life Cycle, continued
1.text: Systems Life Cycle, continued. A model change is a release: re-run the evals before and after, because behavior can change between model versions (Module eight).

1.title: REST APIs and JSON
1.text: R E S T A P I s and Jason. The Claude A P I is a R E S T A P I over H T T P S with Jason request and response bodies. You send a P O S T with headers (A P I key, version) and a Jason body; the client S D K s (software development kit) wrap this. Know the status code classes: four X X means the request is wrong or not allowed (do not retry unchanged), five X X or an overloaded response means a transient server condition (retry with backoff), four hundred twenty-nine means a rate limit (honor retry-after).

1.title: REST APIs and JSON, continued
1.text: R E S T A P I s and Jason, continued. Idempotency: a retry must not repeat a side effect. A model call is safe to repeat; a tool that charges a card is not, so give tool actions an idempotency key.

1.title: Asynchronous programming
1.text: Asynchronous programming. Calls to Claude are slow (seconds), so use async I O (async or await, an async client) to run many requests concurrently instead of one after another. Bound the concurrency with a semaphore or a worker pool: too many parallel calls cause four hundred twenty-nine errors (Module three). Add exponential backoff with jitter for retries. Streaming (server-sent events) shows text as it arrives and helps perceived latency; the code consumes events as an async stream.

1.title: Asynchronous programming, continued
1.text: Asynchronous programming, continued. The figure shows this: Sequential calls add up; bounded concurrency overlaps them; unbounded concurrency hits rate limits.

1.title: Version control, SDLC integration, code review, refactoring
1.text: Version control, S D L C integration, code review, refactoring. Version control. Commit prompts, schemas, tool definitions and Claude dot M D; never commit A P I keys; use branches and pull requests. S D L C integration. Run evals and tests in C I C D (continuous integration and continuous delivery); use Claude Code in pipelines (dash p) for review and test generation. Code review. Review prompt and tool changes like code; use an independent Claude instance, not the one that wrote the change, for A I-assisted review. Small refactors. Direct edits with tests running; one change at a time.

1.title: Version control, SDLC integration, code review, refactoring, continued
1.text: Version control, S D L C integration, code review, refactoring, continued. Large refactors. Plan first (explore, then plan), write or keep tests, change in small verified steps, review diffs; use plan mode in Claude Code. Exam tip: A refactor touching many files is made safe by tests first and small, verified steps, with a plan before edits.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Requirements: Functional (what), non-functional (how well: latency, cost, quality, security), infrastructure (where: platform, region, limits, secrets). Acceptance criteria: Measurable; they become evals. Trade-off: Quality, latency, cost; the binding constraint decides. Life cycle: Requirements to design to build to test (evals) to deploy to operate to maintain to retire. Prompts: Code: version, review, test, roll back; pin model versions. R E S T or Jason: four X X do not retry unchanged; five X X or overload retry with backoff; four hundred twenty-nine honor retry-after. Async: Bounded concurrency, backoff with jitter, streaming for perceived latency. Version control: Commit prompts and config, never keys; P R s (pull request). Refactoring: Plan, tests first, small verified steps; independent review.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Tidewater's business goal is "faster answers for adjusters". Which statement is a measurable non-functional requirement? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A non-functional requirement states a measurable quality such as latency with a threshold; the others are vague or are design choices.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A requirement says claim files must be processed only in a specific geographic region. Which kind of requirement is this, and what does it influence? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Data residency is an infrastructure requirement that constrains where requests run.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A team ranks its constraints: cost first, answers needed by the next morning, quality must be good. What does this point to? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Cost-first, latency-tolerant work fits batch processing; model size follows the quality bar proven by evals.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Which life-cycle practice makes a prompt change safe to release? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Prompts are code: version them and test them with evals before and after the change.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A provider announces that the model your application uses will retire in six months. What should the team do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A model change is a release; test it with evals and migrate before the date.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. An application sends five hundred independent requests one after another and takes too long. What is the most effective improvement? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Concurrency overlaps the waiting time; bounding it and backing off avoids rate-limit errors.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A tool that issues a refund fails with a network timeout, and the application retries it. What protects the customer? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Idempotency prevents a repeated side effect when a call is retried.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. A developer commits A N T H R O P I C A P I K E Y in a configuration file. What is the right action? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A committed secret is compromised: rotate it and keep keys out of version control.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. A change touches sixty files across a service. Which approach is safest with Claude Code? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Large refactors need a plan, tests and small steps.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. Select two. Which two belong in a requirements list for the claims assistant? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and C. Functional and infrastructure requirements are concrete and testable; the other items are cosmetic or unachievable.

2.title: Practice Question 11
2.text: Question eleven. Select two. Which two practices keep A I-assisted code review reliable? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and E. An independent reviewer and automated tests catch what self-review misses.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all eleven answers. Question one: A. Question two: D. Question three: A. Question four: B. Question five: C. Question six: A. Question seven: C. Question eight: B. Question nine: B. Question ten: B and C. Question eleven: A and E. In the next module, we continue the course.
